masterclass.name: MasterClass
masterclass.verdict: MasterClass's main membership is best treated as inspiration and craft insight from famous practitioners, not as a credential. Every plan unlocks the full library; you pay more only for extra simultaneous devices and offline viewing. Career-focused certificate courses are sold separately.
facts: Annual membership: Standard $10/mo, Plus $15/mo, Premium $20/mo, billed annually ($120, $180, $240 a year)
Not shown on the plan pages we checked
Standard 1; Plus up to 2 simultaneous streams; Premium up to 6

Main membership: not credential-focused. MasterClass Certificates are a separate paid product: 15–20-hour courses with a capstone project and shareable certificate, from $299 per course or a Certificates Annual Pass
Auto-renews; renewal notice sent 30 days before
masterclass.good: Curious learners who enjoy polished, documentary-style lessons and want breadth across cooking, writing, music, business and more. Plus or Premium suits households because of extra streams and profiles.

masterclass.take: Pick Standard if you watch alone online; Plus if two people share or you want offline downloads. Set a reminder before the renewal date, since the plan auto-renews.

brilliant.name: Brilliant
brilliant.tagline: 2 free lessons a day, then Premium
brilliant.verdict: Brilliant Free gives you 2 keys a day. Each key opens one concept or one practice set, then you wait until midnight. Premium removes that cap. On 20 Nov 2026 the subscribe page showed annual list prices of $20 a month for one person and $40 a month for a family of 6, with a Black Friday price of $14 and $28.
facts: Premium is sold monthly, yearly and as a family plan for up to 6 people. A free account remains.

Annual list price on the subscribe page, 20 Nov 2026: individual $20 a month and family $40 a month for 6 seats, each billed as one yearly payment. The same page showed a Black Friday 30% discount at $14 and $28 a month. The page data also included a $30 monthly individual amount with that seasonal discount attached. A monthly family dollar amount was not printed in the view we checked, so we are not repeating the $60 figure from 15 Oct as current.
Premium: unlimited lessons and practice, full access to the Koji tutor, no ads, the ability to jump to any lesson, on web, iOS and Android.

2 keys a day. Each key unlocks one concept or one practice set and the keys reset at midnight in your time zone. You have to take topics in order, ads can appear between concepts, and Koji is only a limited preview.
No trial length was shown on the 20 Nov subscribe page. Brilliant's help index says trials are sometimes offered.
Not advertised on the subscribe page or the pricing help articles we checked.
brilliant.good: People who like short problem-solving sessions in math, science, computer science or data, and who will bump into the 2-key wall. Two concepts a day is a real habit. It is a slow way to finish a course. The family plan at the $40 a month annual list price is $480 a year for 6 seats, or $80 a seat, which is the number to compare with buying separate individual plans.
brilliant.bad: Anyone who needs a certificate, a coding career path, or several hours of new material in one evening. Free Brilliant will stop you after two concepts. If you want to write code in a browser, Codecademy is the closer match. See Brilliant vs Codecademy.
brilliant.take: Stay on the free plan until the 2-key limit annoys you. If you then want a year, the list price we could read was $240 ($20 times 12). During the Black Friday display on 20 Nov that annual charge was shown as $14 a month, which is $168 for the year. Treat $168 as a sale price, not as the renewal price. Brilliant's help centre says it rarely discounts Premium, and names the annual Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale as the main exception.
sources: Brilliant Help: free vs Premium (updated Oct 30, 2026)
Brilliant Help: how much Premium costs (updated Oct 30, 2026)
Brilliant Help: pricing and plans index
brilliant.extra:
What two keys a day allows

Brilliant's free-versus-Premium article, last updated 30 Oct 2026 and re-read on 20 Nov, is specific. A free account gets 2 keys each day. One key opens one concept or one practice set. When both keys are used, you stop until midnight in your time zone. You also cannot skip ahead, and ads can sit between concepts. Koji, the tutor inside the lessons, is a preview that runs out.

Premium, on the same article and on the pricing article (also updated 30 Oct 2026), drops the keys, drops the ads, lets you open any lesson, and includes Koji for the session. Both free and Premium can use the lessons on the web, iOS and Android. The pricing article no longer prints dollar amounts. It tells you to open the subscribe page, which is where the figures below come from.

List price and the 20 Nov sale

Brilliant subscribe page, United States, 20 Nov 2026

udacity.name: Udacity
udacity.tagline: $249 a month on the support FAQ
udacity.verdict: Udacity's support FAQ, re-read on 20 Nov 2026, still says the subscription is $249 a month, or $846 if you pay for four months up front. You cannot buy a single Nanodegree on its own. The public plans page did not print a dollar amount in the page we fetched. It described a monthly plan and a 4-month bundle that converts to month-to-month.
facts: One subscription for the catalog. The support FAQ prices it at $249 a month, or $846 paid up front for four months (it calls that a 15% saving). The plans page, the same day, left the dollar figures as "Loading" and said a discount applies to the first 4 months, after which the plan converts to month-to-month.
No free catalog on the FAQ or the plans page. The FAQ says personalised offers and periodic sales exist for some learners.
The FAQ says Udacity does not support enrollment in an individual Nanodegree or course. The subscription is the product.

The FAQ describes over 80 Nanodegree programs, about 2 to 6 months each depending on weekly hours, and over 300 courses that can often be finished in under a month. The catalog changes: content is added and removed during an active subscription.

A Nanodegree certificate comes after you pass the program's projects. The plans page calls the credential a Udacity-verified certification and says it is included on individual, team and enterprise plans.
The FAQ says you can pause the subscription when you have met a goal, and come back later. It does not describe a refund window.
udacity.good: Someone who can put real weeks into one Nanodegree and wants project reviews, not just videos. At the FAQ's four-month price, $846 is the bill for a program the FAQ itself says often takes two to six months. Four months of $249 would be $996, and $846 is $150 less, which is the 15% the FAQ claims (150 divided by 996).
udacity.bad: Casual learners, and anyone comparing it with a broad catalog subscription. Coursera Plus was $399 for a year at our last full read of that plan. Udacity's four-month FAQ price is already more than twice that, and it does not become a cheap second year: the plans page says the 4-month deal converts to month-to-month. If you only need one Python course, look at Codecademy or a single Udemy course instead.
udacity.take: Treat $249 and $846 as the prices Udacity's own support FAQ still publishes, not as a number we saw painted on the plans page on 20 Nov. Open udacity.com/plans and read the checkout, because the FAQ also mentions personalised offers. If the four-month bundle is what you want, finish inside those four months. The footnote on the plans page says the discount applies to the first 4 months and then the membership goes month-to-month.
sources: Udacity Support: subscription FAQ ($249 a month, $846 for four months)
udacity.extra:
The support FAQ and the plans page do not match in form

We opened both on 20 Nov 2026. The subscription FAQ is blunt: a monthly subscription is $249, and paying $846 up front for four months saves 15%. The same article later says students subscribe monthly or annually. It does not explain how "annual" relates to the four-month price. We are leaving both wordings here so the conflict is visible.

The plans page described three products in the HTML we could read: a monthly subscription, a 4-month subscription it called the best value, and team plans. The dollar slots said "Loading". Two footnotes were readable. A discount applies to the first 4 months, then the plan converts to month-to-month. The 4-month total is framed around the average time to complete a Nanodegree. Individual plans include the content library, hands-on projects, human project feedback, and a Udacity-verified certification, according to the comparison table on that page.

What $846 is being compared with

A four-month Udacity bill against a year of Coursera Plus
Udacity, support FAQCoursera Plus, our last read of that plan
Sticker$249 a month, or $846 for the first four months$59 a month, or $399 a year
What you can enrol inAny Nanodegree or course while the subscription is active. Not one program by itself.Most of the Coursera catalog. Degrees are separate.
CertificateNanodegree certificate after the projects are passedCourse and professional certificates from the partner that built the course

The arithmetic on Udacity's own four-month claim: 249 times 4 is 996, and 996 minus 846 is 150, which is 15.1% off. That checks out against the "save 15%" line. It is a discount on the first four months, not a permanent rate, if the plans-page footnote is the rule the checkout uses.

The FAQ's catalog description is the other concrete figure. It says there are over 80 Nanodegree programs, usually about two to six months, and over 300 shorter courses. A Nanodegree certificate requires passing the projects. You can be enrolled in more than one thing at a time while the subscription is active. If you finish early, the FAQ says you can pause rather than keep paying. It does not promise a refund of the months you did not use.

The head-to-head write-up is Udacity vs Coursera. For cheaper ways to practice code before spending $249, see best platforms to learn coding and tech and the price tracker.

futurelearn.name: FutureLearn
futurelearn.verdict: FutureLearn Unlimited, on the page we read on 20 Nov 2026, is $349.99 billed annually, shown as $29.17 a month. The $244.99 offer from our October checks was not on that page. Unlimited includes a digital Certificate of Achievement on the short courses it covers, and it excludes microcredentials, degrees and ExpertTrack subscription courses.
facts: Unlimited is an annual subscription. The page we checked showed one price, not a separate monthly total. One-off upgrades for single courses still exist, priced on each course.
$349.99 a year, displayed as $29.17 a month, on 20 Nov 2026. No introductory price was printed on the page. The $244.99 figure from October was not there.
Unlimited renews automatically. FutureLearn says it emails three days before renewal. Cancel before the period ends and you keep access until that period ends.

The Unlimited page says 1,400+ short courses from 200+ institutions. Unlimited does not include Paid Upfront courses (microcredentials and degrees), Subscription Access courses inside an ExpertTrack, or program assessments. Open taster courses for degrees are included.

A printable digital Certificate of Achievement on included short courses, once you are eligible. If you cancel, you keep those certificates and you keep access to the courses where you earned one. Other courses go back to a free-learner experience. The Unlimited page does not say the certificate is university credit.
futurelearn.good: Someone who wants a stack of short university courses for a year and cares about keeping the certificate afterwards. At $349.99, Unlimited is $49.01 less than the $399 Coursera Plus annual price from our October read of Coursera. The catalogs are not the same product. FutureLearn's own page puts the count at 1,400+ short courses and names what is left out.
futurelearn.bad: Learners who need a microcredential, a degree, or an ExpertTrack. Those are outside Unlimited, and buying Unlimited will not unlock them. It is also a weak choice if you wanted the October discount: $244.99 was not on the page on 20 Nov, so budget $349.99 unless the checkout shows something lower that day.
futurelearn.take: Ignore old screenshots of a 30% Unlimited offer unless the live page shows it. The number on 20 Nov was $349.99 for the year. Before you pay, filter the short-course list to "Included in Unlimited" and see whether the courses you want are in that set. After you earn a Certificate of Achievement, cancelling does not take that course away. That is the useful part of the renewal terms, and it is spelled out on the Unlimited page. The wider comparison is FutureLearn vs Coursera.
futurelearn.extra:
The October discount was not on the page

On 15 Oct and again on 28 Oct, FutureLearn's Unlimited page showed a $349.99 list price and a $244.99 offer. On 20 Nov 2026 the same URL showed one figure: $29.17 a month, $349.99 billed annually. There was no struck-through price and no "30% off" line. We are retiring $244.99 as a current price. If a sale returns, it will be on that page, not in this paragraph.

$29.17 times 12 is $350.04, a few cents over the $349.99 billed total. The page is showing a rounded monthly equivalent of the annual charge, not a $29.17 bill you can pay twelve separate times. We did not see a distinct monthly Unlimited price.

What the $349.99 does not buy

The Unlimited page is explicit about the holes. You get stand-alone short courses that offer a Certificate of Achievement. You do not get Paid Upfront courses, and the page names microcredentials and degrees in that group. You do not get Subscription Access courses that sit inside an ExpertTrack. You do not get program assessments. Degree taster courses that are open to anyone are included. The practical test is the filter labelled Included in Unlimited. A course card without that label is a separate purchase.

The page also says the subscription covers 1,400+ courses and more than 200 institutions. That is FutureLearn's count, from the page, not a catalog we inventoried.

What you keep if you cancel

Renewal is automatic, with an email three days before. Cancel before the period ends and access runs to the end of the period you paid for. Then three things happen, in the page's own split:

  • You keep every Certificate of Achievement you have earned.
  • You keep Unlimited-style access to each course where you earned one.
  • Courses where you did not earn a certificate go back to the free-learner experience.

If you resubscribe later, the page says you regain the courses from the last subscription. That makes Unlimited less of a cliff than a rental that locks the door on every file. It still is not a reason to pay for a year of courses you have not looked at. Coursera Plus at $399 a year is the nearest wide subscription, and FutureLearn vs Coursera puts the certificate rules next to each other. Both prices are in the price tracker.

babbel.name: Babbel
babbel.verdict: Babbel's own review page, read on 20 Nov 2026, still prices a 12-month plan at $107.40 ($8.95 a month), six months at $80.70 and lifetime at $299.99. Full lessons are paid and ad-free. The first lesson of every course is free, and Babbel Live is no longer sold to individual learners.
facts: Subscriptions paid in advance for a set period, plus a one-time Lifetime plan. Babbel's pricing help article says the price also depends on your country and on whether you buy from Babbel, a partner site, Google or Apple.

On Babbel's review page, 20 Nov 2026: 6 months at $13.45 a month ($80.70 billed each 6 months), 12 months at $8.95 a month ($107.40 for the year), Lifetime $299.99 once. The page says 1-month and 3-month plans exist but does not print those totals. The $17.95 and $45.75 figures from our 15 Oct read of the prices app were not re-confirmed, because that page returned no prices without JavaScript.
Registration is free, and the first lesson of every course is free to try. Full courses need a subscription. Babbel says the lessons carry no ads.
Lessons of about 10 to 15 minutes, built around practical conversation, written for the learner's native language. 14 languages.
No course certificate on the pages we checked.

Renews for the same period unless you cancel before the renewal date. You keep access until the time you already paid for ends. Deleting the app does not cancel the subscription. The help articles we read do not state a money-back window.
babbel.good: Adults who want short, structured dialogue lessons and will actually open the app most weeks. At the 12-month price on Babbel's review page, a year is $107.40, which is less than Rosetta Stone's $159 yearly plan, with the caveat below about how many languages that Babbel plan includes.
babbel.bad: Anyone who needs a free full course, a certificate, or a live teacher. Babbel's review page says Babbel Live is no longer available for individual consumers. It is also a poor fit if you want dozens of languages in one obvious bundle: see the disagreement between Babbel's own pages, described under the next heading.
babbel.take: Read the checkout label before you pay for a year. If it is one language, lifetime at $299.99 is the only Babbel product their review page describes as covering every language, and it costs about 2.8 years of the 12-month plan. If the checkout says all languages, the 12-month plan is the simpler buy and lifetime is a bet that you will still be using Babbel in year three. Start with the free first lesson, or with Duolingo if you are not ready to pay.
sources: Babbel review page (plans, 14 languages, lesson length, Babbel Live)
Babbel Help: try Babbel for free
babbel.extra:
Two official pages disagree on languages

This is the part worth slowing down for. Babbel's review page, read on 20 Nov 2026, says each language needs its own subscription unless you buy lifetime access. The subscriptions help article describes an "All languages" subscription for the whole self-study catalog, and lists Lifetime as a separate choice. Both pages are Babbel's. We are not going to pretend they say the same thing. Open the checkout and read whether the plan name is one language or all 14 before you enter a card.

The 14 languages named on the review page are Spanish (Spain and Mexico are separate courses), French, German, Italian, Portuguese, Dutch, Swedish, Norwegian, Danish, Polish, Turkish, Russian, Indonesian and English. An English speaker learning Spanish does not get the same course as a French speaker learning Spanish: Babbel says each course is written for the learner's native language.

Rosetta Stone, yearly$159 billed once for the year ($13.25 a month)All 25 languages on one subscription, on the plans page
DuolingoThe course content is free, with ads and limitsMany more languages, and less explicit grammar

We are not reprinting the 1-month and 3-month totals from 15 Oct ($17.95 and $45.75). The pricing help article also warns that Google and Apple charges can differ from the website.

What you can try without paying

The free-lesson article says you can register at no cost and open the first lesson of every course. That is enough to hear whether the dialogue style suits you. It is not a free catalog. The same article says Babbel runs no ads, and it credits a team of over 150 experts for the courses. We are citing that as Babbel's description, not as an independent headcount.

If you wanted a teacher on a video call, stop here. Babbel's review page says Babbel Live is no longer available for individual consumers. For the free-versus-paid choice, read Babbel vs Duolingo, then best language learning apps, which adds Rosetta Stone. alison.name: Alison
alison.tagline: free to finish, pay only for the certificate
alison.verdict: Alison still lets you study and finish a course without paying. The certificate help article, marked updated the day before we read it on 20 Nov 2026, says you need 70% on every assessment, a free Learner Record is enough to show you finished, and a digital or parchment certificate is a separate purchase in the Shop. The article does not print the Shop prices.
facts: Courses are free to study and complete. Certificates are optional purchases. The help article points to the Shop for the amounts and does not list them.
Study every section and sit the assessments at no charge. A Learner Record of a finished course is free. You do not have to buy a certificate to have finished.
Complete every section (a green tick on each) and score at least 70% on each assessment. That rule is in the certificate help article.

After you pass, a digital certificate or a mailed parchment can be bought in the Shop. Some courses include a free digital certificate. The certificate language is the language of the final assessment. A purchased certificate carries a QR code that opens a verification page.

The help article says digital certificates bought in the Alison app can be paid with Apple Pay or Google Pay only. The browser Shop also offers card, PayPal and bank transfer. Printed certificates need a full delivery address.
alison.good: A learner who wants a structured free course and can live with a Learner Record, or who will pay the Shop price only if a specific employer has said an Alison certificate counts. The 70% rule is at least a real bar, unlike a certificate that appears for pressing play.
alison.bad: Anyone who needs a university transcript or a professional licence. Alison's certificate is Alison's. It is also a clumsy fit if you care which language is printed on the certificate and you sit the final quiz in the wrong one: the help article says you must retake the assessment in the other language and score higher than before. A parchment already posted is not reprinted. You place a new order.
alison.take: Finish the course free, download the Learner Record, and only then open the Shop. Do not assume a dollar amount from an old review. The help article we read refuses to state one and sends you to the Shop, where the price can move. If the goal is a free school curriculum with no certificate upsell, Khan Academy is the cleaner product. If you want a free audit and a paid university-style certificate, compare edX in best free online course platforms.

alison.extra:
The 70 percent rule

Alison's certificate article was marked "Updated yesterday" when we opened it on 20 Nov 2026. The completion rule is concrete. Every section needs a green tick, and every assessment needs a score of at least 70%. Until both are true, there is nothing in the Shop to buy.

The "is Alison really free" article still says you can study and finish without paying, and that a Learner Record can be downloaded. The certificate article repeats the point in plainer words: you do not have to purchase a certificate in order to certify. The Learner Record is the free proof. The digital file and the parchment are souvenirs you pay for.

The language trap on the certificate

The certificate language is chosen for you. It is the language you used for the final assessment. If you want a different language on the certificate, you retake that assessment in the other language, and the language updates only if the new score is higher than the old one. The digital file then switches. A parchment that has already been dispatched does not. The article says you would place a new order, and it tells you to check the language before you pay so you are not charged twice.

Check the name spelling in the Shop before you pay as well. The article walks through an Edit Name step and warns that a correction later costs extra. We are not quoting a correction fee, because the article does not state one.

How the Shop takes payment

In a browser, the article lists credit or debit card, PayPal, and bank transfer. In the app, digital certificates and digital diplomas are limited to Apple Pay or Google Pay, which the article attributes to Apple and Google rules. If you do not have those, it says to switch to the browser. Printed certificates need a delivery address, and the article suggests a postcode and a PO Box.

A bought certificate or diploma includes a QR code. Scanning it opens an Alison page that shows the credential. The transcript has a verification link too. That is useful if an employer asks whether the PDF is real. It does not make the certificate a degree. For free platforms side by side, use best free online course platforms. Alison's prices, such as they are, stay as "see the Shop" in the price tracker until the help centre prints a number.

teachable.name: Teachable
teachable.tagline: creator school platform, not a curated catalog
teachable.verdict: Teachable is built for creators who sell courses, coaching and downloads under their own brand. It is not a single curated catalog like Coursera or Udemy: each Teachable school sets its own prices, content quality and learner refund rules.
facts: Creators and education businesses running their own school; learners buy from individual schools, not from a Teachable-wide storefront
Starter $39/mo, Builder $89/mo, Growth $189/mo billed monthly; or Starter $29/mo, Builder $69/mo, Growth $139/mo billed annually (22% less than month to month). Custom plans are quote based
7-day free trial on the plans Teachable lists; Teachable says it is a paid service with no free plan
30-day money-back guarantee on Teachable plans (per pricing page FAQ)
Starter lists a 7.5% sales transaction fee; Builder, Growth and Custom list 0% Teachable transaction fees when using Teachable Payments (payment processor fees still apply)
A published course, coaching offering or digital download counts as one product. Starter lists 5 products; Growth lists 50 products on the pricing page
Course certificates appear among Growth plan features on Teachable's pricing comparison; availability still depends on how each school configures its courses
Price, access length and refund terms are set by each school, not by a single Teachable learner policy
teachable.good: Instructors who want to sell under their own brand, keep student relationships, and pick a plan that matches how many products they publish. Annual billing is the clearer value if the school will stay on Teachable for most of a year.
teachable.bad: Learners hoping for one vetted catalog with uniform quality and refunds. Teachable schools vary widely; a course page on Teachable is only as strong as the creator behind it. Also a poor fit if you only need a single consumer subscription for browsing many topics.
teachable.take: If you are a creator, start from Teachable's pricing page, count how many live products you need, and weigh Starter's 7.5% fee against Builder or Growth. If you are a learner who landed on a Teachable checkout, read that school's refund policy before you pay, and compare curated alternatives such as Udemy or LinkedIn Learning when you want platform-level standards.

rosetta-stone.verdict: Rosetta Stone's plans page, read on 20 Nov 2026, charges $19.99 a month or $159 for the year, and that subscription includes all 25 languages. The yearly plan costs less than eight months of the monthly plan. A lifetime subscription is still described in a support article, but neither that article nor the plans page printed a lifetime price.
facts: Monthly or yearly subscription for one person. A lifetime subscription is described in Rosetta Stone's support centre, without a price on the pages we checked.
$19.99 a month billed monthly, or $13.25 a month billed yearly as $159. The plans page labels the yearly option as save 33%.
Not listed on the plans page we checked on 20 Nov 2026.

Immersion lessons, the TruAccent speech tool, Chat Missions for conversation practice, 500+ flashcard sets, and Sapphire Studio for making your own materials. The plans page says one subscription covers all 25 languages.

The plans page lists Spanish (Spain), Spanish (Latin America), German, French, Italian, Dutch, Arabic, Korean, Swedish, Japanese, Hebrew, Chinese, Greek, Persian, Turkish, Russian, Vietnamese, Hindi, Portuguese (Brazil), Filipino (Tagalog), Irish, Latin, English (American), English (British) and Polish.

Not advertised on the plans page we checked.
rosetta-stone.good: A learner who wants several languages on one bill and likes immersion without translation drills. $159 a year for 25 languages is the clean comparison with Babbel, whose review page prices 12 months at $107.40 and then argues with its own help centre about whether that plan is one language or all of them.
rosetta-stone.bad: A tight budget, or anyone who wants a certificate. There is no free tier on the plans page we opened. Nineteen dollars and ninety-nine cents a month with no printed refund window is an expensive way to discover you will not keep the habit. Try Duolingo first if you are unsure.
rosetta-stone.take: The yearly plan is the one that matches how the product is priced. $159 divided by $19.99 is 7.95, so the annual bill costs less than paying monthly once you are in month 8. The plans page's "save 33%" line also checks: twelve months at $19.99 is $239.88, and $159 is about 34% less. Do not buy a lifetime plan from a third-party seller on the strength of the support article. That article defines the term and does not list a current price.
sources: Rosetta Stone Support: lifetime subscription (bylined January 12, 2026)
rosetta-stone.extra:
Eight months is the break-even

The plans page on 20 Nov 2026 showed two numbers and a language list, not a maze of promo codes. Monthly is $19.99, charged every month. Yearly is $159, shown as $13.25 a month, with a "save 33%" label. Twelve times $19.99 is $239.88. The difference is $80.88, which is 33.7% off the monthly run-rate. That is the label, rounded.

Divide 159 by 19.99 and you get 7.95. From the eighth month, the yearly plan has cost less than staying on monthly. If you might quit in month three, monthly is the smaller loss, and only if you actually cancel. The plans page we read did not state a refund window.

What the $159 includes

The same page says the subscription is all-access: all 25 languages, not a pick-one model. It names immersive lessons, TruAccent, Chat Missions, more than 500 flashcard sets, and Sapphire Studio. The 25 names on the page are Spanish from Spain, Spanish from Latin America, German, French, Italian, Dutch, Arabic, Korean, Swedish, Japanese, Hebrew, Chinese, Greek, Persian, Turkish, Russian, Vietnamese, Hindi, Portuguese from Brazil, Filipino (Tagalog), Irish, Latin, American English, British English and Polish.

Set that beside Babbel. Babbel's review page, the same day, priced 12 months at $107.40 and lifetime at $299.99, and said each language is a separate subscription unless you buy lifetime. Rosetta Stone's plans page does not make you have that argument: 25 languages are in the subscription description. Babbel is cheaper for a year if one language is all you want. Rosetta Stone is the simpler bill if you want more than one. The three-way version is best language learning apps.

Lifetime, without a price

Rosetta Stone's lifetime article, bylined 12 Jan 2026, is still up. It says lifetime means access for as long as the products and services you purchased remain available and supported, that the license is for one person, and that it cannot be transferred. It tells you to read the terms. It does not say how many dollars lifetime costs today, and the plans page we opened did not show a lifetime box either. If a lifetime offer appears at checkout, the price on that screen is the price. We do not have a second number to quote.

kajabi.name: Kajabi
kajabi.tagline: Basic is $179 a month, 0% revenue share
kajabi.verdict: Kajabi is a creator platform, not a course catalog. On 21 Nov 2026 its pricing page listed Basic at $179 a month, Growth at $249 and Pro at $499, each with a 14-day trial and a 30-day money-back guarantee. The page says Kajabi takes no revenue share. US card rates on the same page are 2.9% + 30¢ on Basic, 2.8% + 30¢ on Growth and 2.7% + 30¢ on Pro.
facts: People selling their own courses, coaching, memberships, downloads or podcasts. A learner does not subscribe to Kajabi. They buy from one creator's site.

Read 21 Nov 2026. Basic $179 a month, or $143 a month billed annually at $1,716 (save $432). Growth $249 a month, or $199 a month billed annually at $2,388 (save $600). Pro $499 a month, or $399 a month billed annually at $4,788 (save $1,200). Each card says 14 days free and a 30-day money-back guarantee.
Plans only in the help centre

The help article Kajabi plans and pricing, which showed Updated yesterday when we opened it on 21 Nov, also lists Kickstarter at $89 a month or $852 a year, and Parked at $29 a month. Those two were not cards on the public pricing page.
The pricing page says 0% revenue share: Kajabi takes no cut of what you sell. Processing fees still apply, and the page says they vary by country and payment provider.

On the pricing comparison, labelled for US entities: Basic 2.9% + 30¢, Growth 2.8% + 30¢, Pro 2.7% + 30¢. A separate fee if you use an outside processor, excluding PayPal and Kajabi Payments: Basic 2%, Growth 1%, Pro 0.5%.
Products you can sell: Basic 5, Growth 50, Pro unlimited. Contacts: 2,500, 25,000 and 100,000. Websites: 1, 1 and 3. A pricing FAQ says extra contacts come in blocks of 25,000 for $125 a month.

Kajabi's US payments article, dated 20 Oct 2026, adds 0.7% on subscriptions and payment plans, on top of the card rate, including the first charge. Refunding a charge does not return the original processing fee. A dispute is $15.
kajabi.good: A creator who will use the site, the email and the checkout, and who would rather pay a card rate than a percentage of every sale. On a one-time $1,000 charge, Basic's US card line is $29.30 (2.9% plus 30¢). Growth is $28.30. Pro is $27.30. Those are the pricing-page rates, before the 0.7% the US article adds when the charge is a subscription. Teachable, re-read the same day, still lists Starter at $39 a month with a 7.5% transaction fee, which is $75 on that same $1,000. The two fees are not the same kind of charge: Teachable's 7.5% sits on top of a processor, and Kajabi's percentage is the card rate itself.
kajabi.bad: A learner looking for a catalog, and a creator with one small product. Basic is $140 a month more than Teachable Starter before anyone buys anything. Until sales are large enough that a 7.5% platform fee hurts more than a $179 subscription, the cheaper plan can be the one with the percentage. Kajabi's own page did not show Kickstarter ($89 on the help article) among the three cards, so do not budget a plan you cannot see at checkout.
kajabi.take: Count products first. Basic stops at 5, Growth at 50, Pro says unlimited. Then read the card rate for the plan, not the 0% headline alone. A banner on the pricing page said "6 MONTH DISCOUNT" for a Black Friday offer and did not print a lower price on the plan cards, so the figures above are the prices that were printed. The creator comparison on this site is the Teachable review. Prices for both sit in the price tracker.
kajabi.extra:
Three cards, and two more plans in the help centre

Kajabi's pricing page, read 21 Nov 2026, shows Basic, Growth and Pro. Annual billing is labelled save 20%. The arithmetic holds. Basic: 179 times 12 is $2,148, the annual total is $1,716, and the difference is $432. Growth: 249 times 12 is $2,988, against $2,388, a $600 gap. Pro: 499 times 12 is $5,988, against $4,788, a $1,200 gap. Each annual price divided by 12 is the monthly figure on the card ($143, $199 and $399).

The plans article in the help centre, marked updated the day before we read it, adds Kickstarter at $89 a month or $852 a year, and a Parked plan at $29 a month with no annual option. It also lists a 5% Stripe fee on Kickstarter when Kajabi Payments is available in your country. None of that was a card on the marketing page. If the checkout does not offer Kickstarter, the $89 figure is a help-centre price, not a button you can press.

What 0% revenue share leaves out

The page says Kajabi takes no cut of a sale. The comparison table then prints the card rate, and it limits that table to US entities. A $1,000 one-time charge at those rates:

US card line on a one-time $1,000 sale, Kajabi pricing page, 21 Nov 2026
PlanCard rateOn $1,000Outside processor, if you do not use Kajabi Payments
Basic2.9% + 30¢$29.302% more, and the processor's own fee
Growth2.8% + 30¢$28.301% more
Pro2.7% + 30¢$27.300.5% more

The outside-processor column excludes PayPal and Kajabi Payments, which is what the pricing page says. The US payments article, dated 20 Oct 2026, adds 0.7% when the charge is a subscription or a payment plan, including the first one. On a $1,000 subscription charge that is another $7, so Basic would be $36.30 before any international or invoicing extra. The same article says a refund does not give the processing fee back, and a dispute is $15. International cards add 1.5%.

Set that next to Teachable, whose pricing page we also opened on 21 Nov. Starter was still $39 a month, or $29 billed annually, with a 7.5% transaction fee on the card. Builder was $89 and Growth $189, with annual equivalents of $69 and $139. A Black Friday layer was on that page too. The useful difference is the shape of the fee, not a single winner. Kajabi Basic costs $140 more per month than Teachable Starter before a sale, and then takes a card rate instead of 7.5% on top of a processor. A creator with a few sales a month should do the sum on their own numbers. The write-up of Teachable's plans is the Teachable review.

The limits that actually stop you

Products you can sell, and the page names courses, coaching, memberships, downloads and podcasts: 5 on Basic, 50 on Growth, unlimited on Pro. Contacts: 2,500, 25,000 and 100,000. The FAQ says you can add contacts in blocks of 25,000 for $125 a month without changing plan. Websites: one on Basic and Growth, three on Pro. The branded app is a Pro row, and the page calls it a $199 a month value. AI credits are 0, 500 and 1,000, with 500 more for $15 a month. A banner over the prices said "6 MONTH DISCOUNT" and did not replace the numbers on the cards. Until a lower figure is printed on the plan itself, these are the prices.
